deferred_gaps: Full text of Jensen 2001 was inaccessible; the Psalm 75 item is restricted to the accessible abstract-level proposal at low confidence.
Kister 2020 full text was inaccessible; the A2 record cites its bibliographic identity and abstract only to establish that a comparative study exists.

Berger (Psalm 7), Bazyliński (Psalm 17), Sheveka (Psalm 21), and Pleins (Psalm 49) were available only through an abstract and/or bibliographic record; their items are limited to narrow claims stated there.
The Psalm 43 article reports manuscript grouping secondhand through Wilson without identifying witnesses; the CKL item relies on the refrain and stanza structure, not direct witness verification.
The Psalm 33 and Psalm 83 full theses were consulted, but proposed literary/canonical settings are not treated as composition dates or proof of direct borrowing.
Psalm 105: full Gillingham article inaccessible; record is restricted to publisher-abstract proposal and requires full-text and human review.
Psalm 46: article pagination conflicts between journal index and university repository/PDF; record follows printed PDF locator and discloses the discrepancy.
Psalm 56 and Psalm 92 source verse numbering counts superscriptions differently from BHF chapter numbering; correspondences are documented.
Psalm 77: exilic date and broad mythological reconstruction not adopted; formal observations only.
Psalm 139: vv. 19–22 integrity dispute remains open; Firth’s unified reading is attributed, not settled.
Psalm 39: illness/cultic setting, redaction history, and literary relations remain debated; no date or use is established.
Psalm 48: proposed pre-exilic/exilic layers and historical occasion remain uncertain; no single attack or archaeological conclusion is asserted.
Psalm 62: Botha's post-exilic exploitation setting is a scholarly reconstruction, not independently established.
Psalm 71: Liess's reading is not biographical evidence or proof of a uniform social role for older people.
Psalm 12: Botha’s Psalms 9–14/Proverbs 30 literary relationship and proposed Persian-period social context are not independently established; no exact date is claimed.
Psalm 28: the final verse’s function and the poem’s social setting remain disputed.
Psalm 35: genre, historical occasion, and Davidic authorship remain unresolved; military and legal imagery are interpreted as a literary pattern.
Psalm 38: body imagery may be literal, figurative, or symbolic; no medical diagnosis is inferred.
Psalm 45: Wendland’s proposal of public royal declamation is not independent evidence of a specific performance event.
Psalm 52: Botha’s late Persian-period setting and wisdom-network reconstruction are attributed proposals; the article does not establish a precise composition date or direct literary dependence.

Psalm 59: Janowski’s evening-to-morning reading is a literary interpretation. The relation of the repeated prayer/refrain and any historical occasion remain unresolved; the superscription is not used to date composition.

Psalms 61 and 63: LeMon’s publisher abstract alone was accessible. Entries report only the abstract’s proposal that the bulla analysis strengthens a royal-voice reading; no bulla details, provenance, independent archaeological conclusion, or full-article argument is claimed.
Psalm 64: Eder’s narratological sequence describes the poem’s literary movement; it does not establish a prose historical event, performance setting, or composition date.
Psalm 65: Botha’s proposed Psalms 65–68 editorial cluster and Zion-to-earth sequence are interpretations, not proof of a specific cultic rite, historical event, or date.
Hebrew/English superscription-based verse numbering differs from BHF verse anchors for these psalm studies; correspondences are recorded in source metadata and the packet.
Psalm 70: Auffret’s full French article was inaccessible; only the publisher’s English and French abstracts support the narrowly reported structural proposal.
Psalm 98: Blunda Grubert’s full article was inaccessible; only the Spanish publisher abstract supports the limited group-level framing.
Psalm 87: Zion’s relation to the named nations and Rautenbach’s status reading remain disputed; her article identifies its origin as an MA seminar paper.
Psalm 58: the relevant Sklarz study is in Hebrew; only its English abstract was accessible, so its structural proposal was not authored as CKL evidence.
Psalm 76: no passage-specific scholarly argument was directly inspected that would support a responsible source-backed addition; event and date claims remain deferred.
